newsitem.title: JAPAN: Followers drank blood of Japan subway attack guru.
newsitem.headline: Followers drank blood of Japan subway attack guru.

text.p: Followers of the doomsday cult blamed for the Tokyo subway gas attack had to drink the sect founder's blood in initiation ceremonies, a former member said on Friday.
Kazuo Konya told the Tokyo District Court he paid $1 million yen ($8,000) to take part in a ceremony at which he drank the blood of guru Shoko Asahara, leader of Aum Shinri Kyo (Supreme Truth Sect).

"I was one of 30 people who paid one million yen each to be taken for an initiation ceremony at the headquarters of the cult near Mount Fuji," Konya said at Asahara's murder trial for the March 1995 sarin nerve gas attack.
Mount Fuji is Japan's sacred mountain about 100 km (65 miles) from Tokyo.
In the attack on Tokyo's subway system, 12 people died and thousands were injured.
"We were led into a room where Asahara was sleeping, dressed in orange. I was given a vial of pinkish liquid -- Asahara's blood. It had a strange taste," Konya said.
"We were then led in threes into a dark room where we were made to listen to a droning noise," he added.
The blood potion was supposed to bring acolytes closer to a mystical state of peace, Konya said.
"They told us it would clear our minds and take us closer to a state of grace. At the time I felt it had an effect. But I later realised it was hypnotism," the former cultist said.
During his testimony, Konya occasionally glanced nervously at Asahara who several times interrupted the evidence with near-incoherent babbling.
Asahara, who has yet to enter a plea in his year-long trial, has several times interrupted proceedings with bizarre behaviour which on three occasions has led to his ejection from court.
At one point on Friday, Asahara shouted he had children outside his marriage with his 38-year-old wife, Tomoko.
"I have 12 children, only six with Tomoko Asahara..." he said.
Konya said he left the sect in 1989, 18 months after joining it, when lawyer Tsutsumi Sakamoto, one of the cult's most vocal opponents, told him he could sue the sect for its practices.
Asahara is also on trial for the 1989 murder of Sakamoto, his wife Satoko and their one-year-old son Tatsuhiko, whose remains were found buried in three separate locations in central Japan.
Asahara, who claims he is an incarnation of the Hindu god Shiva, is on trial on a total of 16 counts, ranging from murder to weapons and drugs production.
If he is found guilty on the murder charges he faces a mandatory death sentence by hanging. ($1=124 yen)
